title: Count unique certified items
statement: Count banks and rates by distinct, independently certified items per type, not rows, which hide repeats, treating an item's variants as that item and keeping them in one split.
example: One bank of 143,026 rows held 49,571 unique candidates and 0 independently certified ones.
detail: An inventory of the AP history question substrate found 143,026 gross rows, 49,571 sampling-eligible unique candidate bodies and 0 independently certified rows, so a claim of 100,000 usable items was rejected (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0170-apush-deliverable-shape-user-pause-checkpoint.qmd`). Its deterministic split kept 606 lineage-connected groups whole, with zero collisions across strata, and its remaining work includes rejecting contamination between training, development and audit sets. Every variant of one item, its paraphrases, number swaps and shared templates, is kept in the same split.
against: The split is discovery evidence, not training, certification or model-performance evidence (the same file). The near-duplicate count hashed only the first 200 characters, so items sharing a passage but asking different questions counted as duplicates, and several questions on one source is normal exam practice (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/data/analysis_report.md`). Variety and pass rate can pull apart: the variety fix was described as 'a quality/variety repair, not a guaranteed score-only patch' (icloud-work/aptraining-crystal-copy-20260521/variant-calibration-lab-snapshot/run_0506c1fd_v2_final_variety_static.md, line 41). Variety needs enough samples to measure: a seven-response smoke showed one duplicate in two set samples, and the lab asked for at least five extra samples of each repeating type before a live check.

For any future expansion, five counts should remain distinct: 1. gross rows discovered; 2. schema-valid rows; 3. content-hash-unique candidate bodies; 4. source-cleared and current-format bodies; 5. package-eligible or serving-eligible bodies.

Item candidates, prompt-response training examples, item contracts, evaluator observations, selected or cache winners, source stimuli, and curriculum facts use different counting units. They are never added together into one “sample” number.

The inventory reports different object kinds separately. Curriculum facts, item contracts, generated candidates, prompt-response training examples, evaluator observations, selected winners, and source stimuli are not additive.

Train, development, audit, and blind holdout splits must be assigned by source or stimulus lineage and near-duplicate group before model exposure. Related variants stay in one split. Otherwise a large corpus can produce impressive evaluation through shared sources or paraphrases rather than generalization.
